definition: Because natural gas is a gas rather than a liquid, it disperses unless kept in a sealed, pressurized location, and holding an economically meaningful amount requires very large storage volumes.
core_idea: Gas takes up far more space than an energy-equivalent liquid fuel, so economically useful storage requires either huge volumes or high pressure, which is why underground reservoirs (with their vast natural capacity) became the dominant storage method.
key_points: Storing the energy equivalent of one gallon of gasoline as natural gas at atmospheric pressure takes about 900 gallons of storage space.
Pressurizing the gas reduces the space needed but still requires a very large facility.
Underground reservoirs are the most common storage location because of their large natural capacity.
relationships: Drives the use of depleted reservoirs, salt caverns, and aquifers as storage types
